The meal that comes second in the day, after breakfast, is lunch.

In "The Sunflower," the author’s motive to explore themes of human connection and the natural cycle of life and decay is structurally linked to the protagonist’s experience. The wilting of the sunflower serves as a botanical metaphor that mirrors the protagonist’s internal state of sadness and isolation. By aligning the physical decline of the plant with the emotional deterioration of the character, the author emphasizes the consequences of neglect, thereby urging readers to reflect on how isolation impacts both personal relationships and the natural world.
